claims.claim: The few hundred confirmations per second aren't the problem; the threads sitting idle are.
claims.about: Spring Boot (Tomcat), with and without virtual threads
claims.measured: java-spring 15,611 req/s and java-spring-vt 14,571 req/s in the 10 ms I/O-wait test at 256 connections on 1 CPU; at least 13,653 req/s in plaintext
claims.why: Spring Boot handled tens of times more than a few hundred requests per second on one CPU, so throughput is not the bottleneck at that rate.

claims.claim: Tomcat's default thread pool is 200, so each pod filled up at about 200 waiting requests.
claims.about: Spring Boot on Tomcat with platform threads
claims.measured: java-spring served 256 connections at 15,611 req/s with 10 ms waits (p50 15.01 ms); no test held requests open long enough to hit a thread limit
claims.why: The 10 ms waits at 256 connections never come close to the point where a 200-thread pool would cap concurrency, so the measurements cannot confirm or refute a ceiling at about 200 waiting requests.

claims.claim: With virtual threads, a waiting request costs a few KB instead of a whole platform thread.
claims.about: Spring Boot with virtual threads on Java 21
claims.measured: java-spring-vt peaked at 444 MB vs 491 MB for java-spring in the I/O-wait test at 256 connections
claims.why: Only total peak memory at 256 connections was measured, which cannot be broken down into a cost per waiting request.

claims.claim: Enabling virtual threads makes the 200-thread limit go away, so the connection limit (12,000) becomes the real ceiling and one pod can hold all 10,000 partners.
claims.about: Spring Boot with virtual threads on Java 21
claims.measured: java-spring-vt reached 14,571 req/s at 256 connections in the I/O-wait test (p50 16.75 ms), slightly below java-spring at 15,611 req/s; nothing was measured above 256 connections
claims.why: The benchmark tops out at 256 concurrent connections with 10 ms waits, so it says nothing about whether one pod can hold 10,000 requests open for 30 seconds each.
